issues.description: The exclusion rate in Experiment 1 is extremely high (17 out of 40 participants, or 42.5%). This suggests either a flawed task design that participants found too difficult or a highly non-representative final sample, which threatens the generalizability of the findings.
issues.quote: 45 participants started training, 5 participants were excluded based on their training results. The remaining 40 participants... Exclusion of participants with too few high confidence critical trials... resulted in an inclusion of 23 participants (5 participants were excluded)

issues.description: Experiment 2 also shows a massive exclusion rate (92 out of 290 participants, or 31.7%). Excluding nearly a third of the sample based on the number of 'high confidence' trials introduces significant selection bias, as the remaining participants may have different metacognitive or memory profiles.
issues.quote: Exclusion of participants with too few high confidence trials in one or more cells of the design (10 trials or less) resulted in an inclusion of 198 participants (92 participants were excluded)

issues.description: The primary finding (pseudo-to-real letter errors) can be explained by a simple response bias toward familiar categories rather than a memory illusion. In a forced-choice task, when memory is slightly degraded, participants are naturally biased to select a valid alphabet member over a mirrored one, regardless of what they 'remember'.
issues.quote: Moreover, high confidence errors occurred mainly for pseudo-to-real letter memories, and much less often for real-to-pseudo-letter memories, indicating that visual similarity is not the primary cause of this memory-bias.

issues.description: The training task used to screen participants (detecting orientation changes in rectangles) is cognitively distinct from the experimental task (identifying mirrored letters). Proficiency in the former does not necessarily ensure 'minimal proficiency' or motivation for the latter.
issues.quote: In this training task, participants were instructed to indicate whether the rectangle at a cued location in a memory display had the same orientation as the rectangle at that same location in a test display.

issues.description: The confidence scale changes between Experiment 1 (1-2) and Experiment 2 (1-4). This makes it impossible to compare 'high confidence' across experiments, as '2' on a 2-point scale is psychometrically different from '4' on a 4-point scale.
issues.quote: After selecting the target letter, participants indicated their confidence by clicking on one of two boxes (from 1-2, 1 = guess, 2 = certain). ... and then indicated her confidence (on a scale from 1 - 4).

issues.description: In Experiment 3, the stopping rule for sequential analysis was a Bayes Factor (BF) of 6. This is a relatively low threshold for evidence, especially in a field concerned with replicability, where a BF > 10 is usually considered the minimum for 'strong' evidence.
issues.quote: Every other day of testing, the sequential analysis was run, and once the outcome crossed a BF of 6, testing would stop.

issues.description: The authors do not account for phonological/verbal encoding. Real letters have names (e.g., 'C'), while pseudo-letters are likely encoded as 'mirrored C'. The 'illusion' may simply be the loss of the 'mirrored' tag in verbal working memory, which is a known phenomenon in memory decay rather than a visual 'illusion'.
issues.quote: Instead ‘world knowledge’ (e.g., which orientation letters usually have) appear to drive these STM illusions.

issues.description: In Experiment 1, the 'interference' display appears 5 seconds after the memory display offset. Given that the 'Short' condition probe occurs at 0.75s, the interference display actually occurs *after* the response in some conditions, or so late that it likely doesn't interfere with the maintenance phase of STM as intended.
issues.quote: If the memory probe appeared in isolation (the Short and Long conditions), the irrelevant second display appeared 5 seconds after memory display offset

issues.description: Experiment 4 was conducted online via Zoom, while Experiments 1-3 were in-lab. Online environments introduce uncontrolled variables (screen size, lighting, distractions) that are not present in lab settings, yet the results are pooled in the general discussion as if conditions were identical.
issues.quote: Second the data was collected in an online experiment, using Neurotask scripting. Participants that signed up to take part in the experiment were invited to join a Zoom meeting

issues.description: The manuscript relies entirely on Bayes Factors and p-values (implied) but fails to report standard effect sizes (e.g., Cohen's d, partial eta-squared). This makes it difficult to assess the practical significance of the 'increase' in illusions over time.
issues.quote: The Bayesian repeated measures ANOVA showed that a model with main effects for Error Type, Target Type, and Memory Delay... had the best fit (BFm = 18)

issues.description: There is a numbering error in the results section. Both the results for Experiment 3 and Experiment 4 refer to 'Figure 5'.
issues.quote: Error rates for confidence trials are shown in Figure 5. ... Figure 5 shows the error rates for high confidence trials. [referring to Exp 4]

issues.description: Participants were 'explicitly instructed not to confuse real and pseudo-letters'. This instruction may have inadvertently signaled to participants that the experiment was about the real/pseudo distinction, potentially inducing demand characteristics or unnatural focus on that specific feature.
issues.quote: They were explicitly instructed not to confuse real and pseudo-letters and received feedback on their performance after each trial.

issues.description: The threshold for excluding participants (10 trials per cell) is arbitrary. If a participant has 9 trials in one cell but 50 in others, they are excluded entirely, which may discard valuable data and bias the sample toward those with specific response patterns.
issues.quote: Exclusion of participants with too few high confidence critical trials in one or more cells of the design (10 trials or less) resulted in an inclusion of 23 participants

issues.description: The study only uses mirroring as a transformation. To claim a general 'STM illusion' driven by world knowledge, other transformations (e.g., rotations, font distortions) should be tested to ensure the effect isn't specific to horizontal symmetry.
issues.quote: Pseudo-letter were mirrored (i.e. flipped from left to right). Therefore only letters that changed when mirrored were included

issues.description: The tables contain repetitive headers (e.g., 'Table 1: error rates ANOVA' repeated 12 times in the text block), which suggests a formatting error or poor data extraction into the manuscript.
issues.quote: Table 1: error rates ANOVA | Table 1: error rates ANOVA | Table 1: error rates ANOVA | Table 1: error rates ANOVA...

issues.description: The authors use 'STM' as an umbrella term but then switch between Iconic, Fragile, and Working Memory. The delays used (0.75s to 3s) are at the very edge of Iconic memory and the start of Working memory, making the claim that these are 'STM illusions' somewhat imprecise regarding which system is failing.
issues.quote: STM is often hypothesized to consist of short-lived (<500 ms) iconic memory and longer lasting working memory.

issues.description: In Experiment 1, the response display included 'none of these', but this was removed in later experiments. This change in task constraints (forced-choice vs. non-forced-choice) significantly alters the cognitive strategy and the likelihood of guessing, yet the experiments are discussed as a continuous set.
issues.quote: They were instructed to select "none of these" if the target letter was not a response option. ... the response option "none of these" was eliminated. [in Exp 2]

issues.description: The use of listwise deletion for a participant in Experiment 3 due to zero high-confidence responses in one cell is a sub-optimal statistical approach. It further reduces an already small sample size and ignores the information that the participant was unable to perform the task with confidence.
issues.quote: Because of listwise deletion of missing values (resulting from 0 high confidence responses in one or more of the cells of the design), one participant was excluded from the main ANOVA.

issues.description: The study assumes 'high confidence' equals 'actual memory'. However, participants may have high confidence in their *inferences* (e.g., 'I saw a C-shape, so it must have been a C'). This is a metacognitive error, not necessarily a change in the visual memory trace itself.
issues.quote: isolating high confidence responses is necessary to identify those responses that reflect a participant having an actual, albeit false, memory

issues.description: The participants are almost exclusively young university students (average age ~20-22). This demographic has peak cognitive performance and high familiarity with standardized testing, which may not reflect how STM illusions function in the general population or older adults.
issues.quote: 40 participants (28 female; age range 19-30 years, average age 22.2 years) ... 290 participants ... average age 20.3 years

issues.description: The use of Matlab 2012b for Experiment 1 (likely conducted much earlier than the others) suggests a very long data collection period or the use of outdated scripts, which may have compatibility issues with modern Psychtoolbox versions.
issues.quote: The experiment was programmed in Matlab version 2012b using the Psychophysics Toolbox routines

issues.description: The authors conclude that their findings support a 'predictive processing' view, but they do not test any specific computational models of predictive coding. The results are equally compatible with simpler models of memory decay and Bayesian integration at the retrieval stage.
issues.quote: Our findings support a predictive processing view of the formation and maintenance of memory

issues.description: In Experiment 2, participants received 'extensive feedback' to keep them motivated. Feedback in a memory task can lead participants to change their response strategy (e.g., becoming more cautious about pseudo-letters), which confounds the measurement of 'natural' memory illusions.
issues.quote: After each block the participant received feedback on her performance which included information about her average accuracy. This extensive feedback was provided to keep the participants motivated.

issues.description: In Experiment 4, the authors mention 'follow-up t-tests' but do not specify if these were Bayesian t-tests or frequentist, nor do they provide the t-statistics or degrees of freedom, only the BFs.
issues.quote: Illusory responses increased from 14% to 19% in the longer delays (BF > 1000 in follow-up t-test)
